sources.note: p. 467 puts 'the dialects spoken in the Iluk... valleys' (Iluk = Nipsan) in the north-western group beside the Yale language of Kosarek; p. 470: 'In Eipomek and in the dialects east of Eipomek, accent is phonemic. Angguruk places the accent on the last syllable, and the Yale language tends to place it on the last syllable.' This is said of Yale (Kosarek, kosa1249), not of Nipsan.

Bibliographic value only: names the existing data as Bromley n.d. unpublished survey vocabulary (unobtained), Voorhoeve 1975: 116 (37 items), and Heeschen 1992 Yale dictionary p. 8 / some Iluk-valley forms.

Nothing on phonology. Alternate names Southern Jale, Yale-Nipsan; 2,500 speakers (1993 R. Doriot); Kurima sub-district west of Hmanggona; lexical similarity 78% with Kosarek Yale, 59% with Nalca; Bible portions 1982; distinct from the three Yali (Dani-family) languages.

sources.citation: Heeschen, Volker. 1978. The Mek languages of Irian Jaya with special reference to the Eipo language. Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya Development 7(2): 3-46. Jayapura: Universitas Cenderawasih / SIL.
sources.note: Only group-level: p. 12 'Stress seems to be partially phonemic in the east, e.g. Ok Bab 'uku fire and aha young plant of sweet potatoes, while tones are said to be phonemic in Nalca and Kosarek (Bromley 1973:15 and Rule and Cutting).' Nipsan is listed p. 7 as '(6) a: Nipsan, b: Yali, c: see map' with no data source of Heeschen's own, and placed p. 10 in the western group with Eipo, Nalca, Korapun, Kosarek; its only data are Bromley's wordlists via Voorhoeve 1975a (p. 8). No statement about Nipsan stress.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Languages of Irian Jaya: Checklist. Preliminary classification, language maps, wordlists. Pacific Linguistics B-31. Canberra: ANU. Entry 122 'Yaly' (Goliath stock-level family, pp. 46-47) and 37-item wordlist '122. YALY (Br)' after Bromley, printed pp. 116-117 (pdf p. 120).
sources.note: Nothing. The Yaly entry gives no dialects, villages or description (sources 'U 12, 13' only); the wordlist uses a unified orthography that is 'neither phonemic nor accurately phonetic' and marks no stress or tone.
